summary: Remove the outermost pair of parentheses from every primitive of a valid parentheses string.
mainInsight: The outer pair of each primitive is the '(' read at depth 0 and the ')' that returns the depth to 0; keep everything else.
invariant: depth equals the number of unmatched '(' in the prefix read so far.

approaches.name: Split into primitives, then strip
approaches.summary: Find primitive boundaries with a balance counter, then slice off first and last characters.

approaches.name: Stack of open parentheses
approaches.summary: Push '(' and pop on ')', keeping a character if the stack is non-empty at the right moment.
weaknesses: The stack stores only identical characters

approaches.name: Depth counter
approaches.summary: Maintain depth and append inner '(' before incrementing and inner ')' after decrementing.
weaknesses: Order of check and update matters

personalSolution.approach: Stack of '(' used as a depth counter
personalSolution.notes: Correct and linear. The stack only stores identical characters, so an integer counter gives the same logic in constant extra space.

commonMistakes: Updating the depth before the check for '(' (keeps the outer '(').
Checking the depth before decrementing for ')'.
Using string slicing in a loop, which makes it quadratic.
edgeCases: A mix of deep and shallow primitives.

promptVariants: How do you recognise the outermost parentheses of each primitive in a single pass?
Why is a depth counter enough to find the outer pair?
cards.answer: Keep the number of currently unmatched '('. A primitive starts when a '(' is read at depth 0 and ends when a ')' brings the depth back to 0. Those two characters are exactly the outer pair, and every other character belongs inside.
cards.explanation: Primitive decomposition is just the points where the depth is zero.

promptVariants: A '(' is kept only if the depth before it is at least ___.
Before incrementing for a '(', it is an inner parenthesis when depth >= ___.
cards.explanation: At depth 0 the '(' opens a new primitive and is the outer one, so it is dropped.

promptVariants: In your loop, why does the ')' pop come before the `if stack` check while the '(' push comes after it?
What would change if you pushed '(' before the `if stack` check?
cards.answer: For ')' we first pop, so an outer ')' leaves the stack empty and is skipped; an inner ')' leaves it non-empty and is kept. For '(' we check before pushing, so an outer '(' sees an empty stack and is skipped. Pushing first would make every '(' look inner and keep the outermost '(' in the output.
cards.explanation: The order of check and update decides which side of the boundary a character falls on.

cards.answer: Only one bracket type exists, so only the count of unmatched '(' matters
cards.explanation: The stack only ever holds identical '(' characters, so its size is all the information it carries; a counter stores exactly that size in constant space.
